# Introduction

This document compares individual tree phenology metrics derived from PlanetScope (PS) imagery with ground-based observations from the USA National Phenology Network (NPN) in urban areas. The goal is **to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of PS-derived phenology relative to ground observations**.

For the remote sensing-based metrics, we focus on the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS), calculated from time series of the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI). For the ground observations, comparable SOS and EOS metrics are derived from individual tree records in the NPN, based on leaf-related phenophases. These metrics are then directly compared with their PS-derived counterparts to assess consistency and potential bias.

# Processing NPN data

## Filter NPN across CONUS cities

The NPN data is downloaded from the [USA National Phenology Network Individual Phenometrics](https://www.usanpn.org/data/observational). I filtered the data to include only tree individuals from urban areas for the years 2016-2024.

The filter rules are:

-   Keep records with `Observed_Status_Conflict_Flag` equal to -9999.
-   Exclude records with functional types: "Algae", "Evergreen forb", "Forb", "Graminoid", "Semi-evergreen forb".
-   Exclude records with `NumDays_Since_Prior_No` or `NumDays_Until_Next_No` greater than 21.
-   Combine series of phenophase observations that are separated by gaps of 21 days (or other threshold) or less.

> It is common that there were multiple instances where the plant transitioned from a status of No to a status of Yes. These can represent real phenomena, for instance a drought deciduous tree that leafs out several times in a year, or a dogwood that reblooms after a frost event. This can also occur when observers are reporting on the same plant on sequential days but are not in agreement on phenophase status with other observers.

```{r}
us_city <- st_read(("~/lab-data/datasets/boundary/USAdministrative/USCities/tl_2024_us_uac20.shp"),quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)
us_boundary <- st_read(("~/lab-data/datasets/boundary/USAdministrative/US/us_boundarydissolve.shp"),quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)
threshold <- 21 # tolerance of gap to combine series

npn <- read_csv(here("data/raw/CONUS/NPN/NPN1624/individual_phenometrics_data.csv"),
                col_types = cols(Latitude = col_double(), Longitude = col_double())) |>
  filter(!Species_Functional_Type %in% c("Algae", "Evergreen forb", "Forb", "Graminoid", "Semi-evergreen forb")) |>
  filter(NumDays_Since_Prior_No > 0 & NumDays_Until_Next_No > 0) |>
  filter(NumDays_Since_Prior_No <= threshold & NumDays_Until_Next_No <= threshold) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
  st_filter(us_city, .predicate = st_within) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(Species = paste0(Genus, " ", Species),
         Phenophase_Description = ifelse(
           Phenophase_Description == "Breaking leaf buds (lilac/honeysuckle)", "Breaking leaf buds", Phenophase_Description)) |> 
  filter(Phenophase_Description != "Young leaves (forbs)", Observed_Status_Conflict_Flag == "-9999")
  
npn_filter <- npn |>
  group_by(Individual_ID, Phenophase_Description) |>
  arrange(First_Yes_Julian_Date) |>
  # compute gap to previous last date
  mutate(
    gap = First_Yes_Julian_Date - lag(Last_Yes_Julian_Date, default = first(First_Yes_Julian_Date)),
    new_series = ifelse(is.na(gap) | gap > threshold, 1, 0),
    series_id = cumsum(new_series)
  ) |>
  group_by(Individual_ID, Phenophase_Description, series_id) |>
  summarise(
    First_Yes_Julian_Date = min(First_Yes_Julian_Date),
    Last_Yes_Julian_Date = max(Last_Yes_Julian_Date),
    First_Yes_Year = min(First_Yes_Year),
    Last_Yes_Year = max(Last_Yes_Year),
    NumYs_in_Series = sum(NumYs_in_Series, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(Length_Series = Last_Yes_Julian_Date - First_Yes_Julian_Date + 1)
```

To select high-quality phenology series, I filter the individuals which have multiple observations over time and multiple phenophases.

-   The average number of 'yes' in a series is greater than 1, which indicates that the series has multiple observations over time, making a more reliable phenophase period.
-   The individual that only has phenophase of "Leaves" is not included, as it alone does not provide enough information for green-up and green-down.
-   The coverage year of an individual is greater than 1, which indicates that the individual has been regular observed in multiple years, making a more reliable sample.

```{r}
npn_filter_individual <- npn_filter |>
  filter(NumYs_in_Series > 1) |>
  group_by(Individual_ID, Phenophase_Description) |>
  summarise(
    Sum_Ys = sum(NumYs_in_Series),
    years_covered = list(
      unique(unlist(map2(First_Yes_Year, Last_Yes_Year, seq)))
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Observe_Year = map_int(years_covered, length),
    Sum_Ys_Per = Sum_Ys / Observe_Year
  ) |>
  filter(Observe_Year > 1)

npn_filter_individual_per <- npn_filter_individual |>
  select(Individual_ID, Phenophase_Description, Sum_Ys_Per) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Phenophase_Description,
    values_from = Sum_Ys_Per
  ) |>
  # count how many phenophases are observed
  mutate(cover_phenophase = rowSums(!is.na(across(-Individual_ID)))) |>
  filter(!(cover_phenophase == 1 & !is.na(Leaves)))

npn_filter_individual_yr <- npn_filter_individual |>
  select(Individual_ID, Phenophase_Description, Observe_Year) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Phenophase_Description,
    values_from = Observe_Year
  ) |>
  # count how many phenophases are observed
  mutate(cover_phenophase = rowSums(!is.na(across(-Individual_ID)))) |>
  filter(!(cover_phenophase == 1 & !is.na(Leaves)))
```

## NPN derived phenology metrics

For the ground-observed individual phenology, NPN offers six leaf-related phenophases : (1) Breaking leaf buds, (2) Young leaves, (3) Increasing leaf size, (4) Leaves, (5) Colored leaves, and (6) Falling leaves. For lilac/honeysuckle, there is one more phenophase "All leaf buds broken". From these, key phenological metrics for individual urban trees could be extracted and compared with PS-derived phenology metrics.

```{r fun-compute-phe-npn}
#| include: false
compute_npnphe <- function(start = "Leaves", end = "Increasing leaf size") {
  npn_filter |>
    filter(
      Individual_ID %in% (
        npn_filter_individual_yr |>
          filter(.data[[start]] >= 1 & .data[[end]] >= 1) |>
          pull(Individual_ID)
      ),
      Phenophase_Description %in% c(start, end)
    ) |>
    mutate(
      year = ifelse(Phenophase_Description == start, First_Yes_Year, Last_Yes_Year)
    ) |>
    group_by(Individual_ID, year, Phenophase_Description) |>
    summarise(
      doy = if (unique(Phenophase_Description) == start) {
        min(First_Yes_Julian_Date, na.rm = TRUE)
      } else {
        max(Last_Yes_Julian_Date, na.rm = TRUE)
      },
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    group_by(Individual_ID, year) |>
    summarise(
      npn_doy = mean(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
      n = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    filter(n == 2) |>
    select(-n) |>
    mutate(
      npn_doy = yday(as_date(npn_doy - 2440588, origin = "1970-01-01"))
    ) |>
    left_join(
      npn |> distinct(Individual_ID, Species,Species_Functional_Type, Longitude, Latitude),
      by = "Individual_ID"
    )
}
```

### Match the `Start of Season (SOS)`

In the remote sensing context, the start of season (SOS) is defined as the day of year (DOY) when the EVI curve for an individual tree first crosses the 50% green-up threshold. This threshold corresponds to the strongest relative signal observed during the green-up phase from satellite imagery. To match the PS-derived SOS, I tested several leaf-related phenophase indicators from NPN, following the approaches proposed by @modis_npn_xin and @ps_npn_zhao.

Case 1.  Mean value of *the first date of "Leaves"* and *the last day of "Increasing leaf size"*.

Case 2.  Mean value of *the first date of "Breaking leaf buds"* and *the last day of "Increasing leaf size"*.

Case 3.  Mean value of *the first date of "Young leaves"* and *the last day of "Increasing leaf size"*.

[@fig-npn-sos-pdf] displays the distribution of SOS derived from NPN data for each case of SOS computation. In the first two cases, the median SOS occurs around 120 (doy), which is reasonable; however, the wide range raises uncertainty about **whether it reflects true biological and geographical variation, or potential observation and calculation error in these metrics**.

```{r fig-npn-sos-pdf}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 16
#| warning: false

npn_sos <- compute_npnphe(start = "Leaves", end = "Increasing leaf size") |>
  mutate(type = "case1") |>
  bind_rows(
    compute_npnphe(start = "Breaking leaf buds", end = "Increasing leaf size") |>
      mutate(type = "case2")
  ) |>
  bind_rows(
    compute_npnphe(start = "Young leaves (tree/shrub)", end = "Increasing leaf size") |>
      mutate(type = "case3")
  ) |>
  mutate(phe = "SOS",
         genus= str_extract(Species, "^[^ ]+"))

ggplot(npn_sos, aes(npn_doy)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), bins = 30, fill = "grey", color = NA) + 
  geom_density(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "DOY",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of NPN-derived SOS"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

[@fig-npn-sos-pdf-sp] shows the histogram of SOS by species and case type. The top 10 species with the most observations are displayed. Similarly, a large degree of variation is observed within each species, suggesting either ecological differences or measurement uncertainties.

### Match the `End of Season (EOS)`

Similarly, for remote sensing, the EOS is defined as the day of year when the EVI curve of an individual tree’s growing season first crosses the 50% green-down threshold. In NPN, I tried several phenophases to match the EOS:

Case 1.  Mean value of *the first date of "Colored leaves"* and *the last day of "Leaves"*.

Case 2.  Mean value of *the first date of "Colored leaves"* and *the last day of "Falling leaves"*.

[@fig-npn-eos-pdf] displays the distribution of EOS derived from NPN data for each case of EOS computation. And [@fig-npn-eos-pdf-sp] shows the histogram of EOS by species and case type. Similarty, the median EOS is reasonable, and the wide range raises uncertainty as well.

```{r fig-npn-eos-pdf}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false
npn_eos <- compute_npnphe(start = "Colored leaves", end = "Falling leaves") |>
  mutate(type = "case1") |>
  bind_rows(
    compute_npnphe(start = "Colored leaves", end = "Leaves") |>
      mutate(type = "case2")
  ) |>
  mutate(phe = "EOS", genus= str_extract(Species, "^[^ ]+"))

ggplot(npn_eos, aes(npn_doy)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), bins = 30, fill = "grey", color = NA) + 
  geom_density(color = "black", size = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "DOY",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of NPN-derived EOS"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Prepare the location for PlanetScope

To prepare the location data for PlanetScope processing, I combined the NPN-derived SOS and EOS datasets, removed duplicate entries, and created a unique identifier for each location. These locations will be used to extract and analyze time series from the PlanetScope imagery.

As demonstrated during the extraction of phenological metrics and in [@fig-npn-individuals], a single location often includes multiple individuals, which sometimes come from different species and functional groups. Therefore, I would like to understand **in data collection how these observations at shared locations are generated and how to handle them**.

# Processing PlanetScope data

PlanetScope, with a spatial resolution of 3 m and a daily revisit cycle, provides an excellent opportunity to capture plant phenology on a large scale and at an individual tree level. The workflow for downloading PlanetScope imagery, processing time-series data, and extracting phenological metrics follows the procedures outlined in the `batchplanet` package and @song_ps.

We focus on the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS), calculated from Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) curves. SOS is defined as the day of year when the EVI curve of an individual tree’s growing season first crosses the 50% green-up threshold. EOS is defined as the day of year when the EVI curve first crosses the 50% green-down threshold. The 50% threshold is used because it represents the point of the most pronounced change in greenness, capturing the strongest relative signal during green-up or green-down (@song_ps).

Due to the PS quota limit, I processed data for only 3 example cities: New York–Jersey City–Newark in NY–NJ (code 63217), Eugene in OR (code 28117), and Corvallis in OR (20422). These 3 cities include 22 locations and 207 individual trees.

>If the validation workflow proves reliable, I will expand the analysis to include all locations in the `npn_points` dataset to conduct a more comprehensive comparison.

# Compare NPN with PlanetScope

## (Better) Summarize by year-location

[@fig-npn-sos-ps] compares the start of season (SOS) dates derived from NPN observations with those estimated from PlanetScope imagery across the first 2 cases (the third case has few smaples). 

The grey dashed 1:1 line indicates perfect agreement. Each point represents the mean NPN SOS for a given location, and the horizontal line ranges show the 5th and 95th percentiles of NPN SOS. Point colors indicate the site (city).

Generally, the trend suggests a consistency between PS-derived SOS and NPN-derived SOS. However, the plot shows that PS SOS tends to be consistently earlier than NPN SOS across locations, as most points fall below the 1:1 line.

```{r fig-npn-sos-ps}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false

library(randomcoloR)
npn_points <- readRDS("~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/StreetTrees/cleaned_ps_input/summary/matching_npn.rds")

# read in all PS_doy_data.rds in the folder
ps_doy_data <- lapply(list.files(here("data/raw/CONUS/NPN/PS_valid/"),
                                 pattern = ".rds", full.names = TRUE), 
                      readRDS) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  filter(doy != "NA") 
npn_sos_ps <- npn_sos |>
  filter(type == "case1") |>
  left_join(npn_points, by = c("Longitude" = "lon", "Latitude" = "lat")) |>
  left_join(ps_doy_data |>
              filter(direction == "up"), by = c("new_id" = "id", "year")) |>
  filter(npn_doy <= 150, doy <= 150, npn_doy >= 0, doy >= 0) |>
  na.omit()
species_npn_sos_ps <- npn_sos_ps |>
  group_by(Species, city, year, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  summarise(
    n(),
    npn_doy = mean(npn_doy),
    doy = mean(doy),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(Species, city, year) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    npn_doy_mean = mean(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    npn_doy_sd = sd(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_mean = mean(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_sd = sd(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    npn_low_bound = npn_doy_mean - npn_doy_sd,
    npn_up_bound = npn_doy_mean +  npn_doy_sd,
    ps_low_bound = ps_doy_mean - ps_doy_sd,
    ps_up_bound = ps_doy_mean +  ps_doy_sd
  )
location_npn_sos_ps <- npn_sos_ps |>
  group_by(city, year, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    npn_doy_mean = mean(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    npn_doy_sd = sd(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_mean = mean(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_sd = sd(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    npn_low_bound = npn_doy_mean - npn_doy_sd,
    npn_up_bound = npn_doy_mean +  npn_doy_sd,
    ps_low_bound = ps_doy_mean - ps_doy_sd,
    ps_up_bound = ps_doy_mean +  ps_doy_sd
  )

npn_eos_ps <- npn_eos |>
  filter(type == "case1") |> # just keep case 1
  left_join(npn_points, by = c("Longitude" = "lon", "Latitude" = "lat")) |>
  left_join(ps_doy_data |>
             filter(direction == "down"), by = c("new_id" = "id", "year")) |>
  filter(npn_doy >= 150, doy >= 150, npn_doy <=365, doy <= 365) |>
  na.omit()
species_npn_eos_ps <- npn_eos_ps |>
  group_by(Species, city, year, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  summarise(
    n(),
    npn_doy = mean(npn_doy),
    doy = mean(doy),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(Species, city, year) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    npn_doy_mean = mean(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    npn_doy_sd = sd(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_mean = mean(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_sd = sd(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    npn_low_bound = npn_doy_mean - npn_doy_sd,
    npn_up_bound = npn_doy_mean +  npn_doy_sd,
    ps_low_bound = ps_doy_mean - ps_doy_sd,
    ps_up_bound = ps_doy_mean +  ps_doy_sd
  )
location_npn_eos_ps <- npn_eos_ps |>
  group_by(city, year, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    npn_doy_mean = mean(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    npn_doy_sd = sd(npn_doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_mean = mean(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    ps_doy_sd = sd(doy, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    npn_low_bound = npn_doy_mean - npn_doy_sd,
    npn_up_bound = npn_doy_mean +  npn_doy_sd,
    ps_low_bound = ps_doy_mean - ps_doy_sd,
    ps_up_bound = ps_doy_mean +  ps_doy_sd
  )

set.seed(20260320)
all_cities <- unique(c(summary_npn_sos_ps$city, summary_npn_eos_ps$city)) |> sort()
color_palette <- setNames(
  randomcoloR::distinctColorPalette(length(all_cities)),
  all_cities
)

# Define a function to fit and plot each case
plot_weighted_fit <- function(df, phe = "SOS", metric = "mean") {
  phe <- match.arg(phe, c("SOS", "EOS"))
  metric <- match.arg(metric, c("mean", "sd"))
  x_var <- paste0("npn_doy_", metric)
  y_var <- paste0("ps_doy_", metric)
  df <- df |> dplyr::filter(is.finite(.data[[x_var]]), is.finite(.data[[y_var]]))

  x <- df[[x_var]]; y <- df[[y_var]]
  r <- if (length(x) >= 3 && sd(x) > 0 && sd(y) > 0)
    cor.test(x, y, method = "pearson") else NULL
  label <- sprintf(" r = %s\n p = %s\nRMSE = %.2f",
                   if (is.null(r)) "NA" else sprintf("%.3f", unname(r$estimate)),
                   if (is.null(r)) "NA" else format.pval(r$p.value, digits = 3),
                   sqrt(mean((y - x)^2)))

  x_lab <- if (metric == "sd") paste0("SD of ", phe, " (NPN, days)") else
    if (phe == "SOS") "Midpoint of first leaf and\nlast increasing leaf size (NPN)" else
      "Midpoint of first colored leaves and\nlast falling leaves (NPN)"
  y_lab <- if (metric == "sd") paste0("SD of ", phe, " (PlanetScope, days)") else
    paste0("Day of 50% ", if (phe == "SOS") "green-up" else "green-down", " (PlanetScope)")

  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = .data[[y_var]]))

  if (metric == "mean"){
    p <- p + 
    geom_segment(aes(x = npn_low_bound, xend = npn_up_bound,
                              yend = .data[[y_var]], color = city),
                          linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.3, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_segment(aes(y = ps_low_bound, yend = ps_up_bound,
                          xend = .data[[x_var]], color = city),
                      linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.3, na.rm = TRUE) }
    

  p +
  geom_point(aes(color = city, size = n), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label,
           hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.2, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = color_palette, limits = all_cities, drop = TRUE) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Sample size", range = c(1, 5),
                        breaks = function(x) round(seq(x[1], x[2], length.out = 3))) +
  guides(
    color = "none",
    size = guide_legend(override.aes = list(color = "grey40", alpha = 0.8))
  ) +
  labs(x = x_lab, y = y_lab) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.80, 0.2),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA),
    legend.key = element_blank(),
    strip.background = element_blank()
  )
}

sp_sos_mean <- plot_weighted_fit(species_npn_sos_ps, phe = "SOS", metric = "mean")
sp_eos_mean <- plot_weighted_fit(species_npn_eos_ps, phe = "EOS", metric = "mean")
loc_sos_mean <- plot_weighted_fit(location_npn_sos_ps, phe = "SOS", metric = "mean")
loc_eos_mean <- plot_weighted_fit(location_npn_eos_ps, phe = "EOS", metric = "mean")
```

## Summarize by year-city-species

[@fig-npn-sos-ps] compares the start of season (SOS) dates derived from NPN observations with those estimated from PlanetScope imagery across the first 2 cases (the third case has few smaples). 

The grey dashed 1:1 line indicates perfect agreement. Each point represents the mean NPN SOS for a given year-city-species, and the horizontal line ranges show the 5th and 95th percentiles of NPN SOS, the vertical line ranges show the 5th and 95th percentiles of NPN SOS. Point colors indicate the site (city). 

Generally, the trend suggests a consistency between PS-derived SOS and NPN-derived SOS. However, the plot shows that PS SOS tends to be consistently earlier than NPN SOS across locations, as most points fall below the 1:1 line.

```{r fig-npn-sos-ps}
set.seed(20260320)

# Define a function to fit and plot each case
plot_weighted_fit <- function(df, phe = "SOS") {
  # model <- lm(doy ~ mean + 0, data = df)
  # df$fitted <- predict(model)

  # slope <- round(coef(model)[1], 3)
  # p_value <- signif(summary(model)$coefficients[1, 4], 3)
  # mse <- mean(residuals(model)^2)
  # rmse <- round(sqrt(mse), 3)
  # annot_label <- paste0("y = ", slope, "x",
  #                       "\np-value = ", p_value)
  cor_res <- cor.test(df$ps_mean, df$npn_mean, method = "pearson")
  r <- round(unname(cor_res$estimate), 3)
  p_value <- signif(cor_res$p.value, 3)
  rmse <- round(sqrt(mean((df$ps_mean - df$npn_mean)^2)), 3)
  annot_label <- paste0("r = ", r,
                        "\np-value = ", p_value,
                        "\nRMSE = ", rmse)

  ggplot(df, aes(y = npn_mean, x = ps_mean)) +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymin = npn_p5, ymax = npn_p95, color = city), linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = ps_p5, xmax = ps_p95, color = city), linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(color = city), alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
    # geom_smooth(
    #   method = "lm",
    #   formula = y ~ x + 0,
    #   se = FALSE,
    #   color = "black",
    #   linewidth = 0.7
    # ) +
    annotate("text",
             x = min(df$ps_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
             y = max(df$npn_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
             label = annot_label,
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 4) +
    scale_color_manual(values = color_palette,
                       limits = all_cities,
                       drop = T) + 
    labs(
      y = paste0("NPN-derived ", phe),
      x = paste0("PlanetScope-derived ", phe)
    ) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.background = element_blank(),
      strip.placement = "outside"
    ) 
}

plot_sos <- plot_weighted_fit(summary_npn_sos_ps, phe = "SOS")
plot_eos <- plot_weighted_fit(summary_npn_eos_ps, phe = "EOS")
```

# Discussion

With the goal of evaluating the accuracy and reliability of PS-derived phenology for urban trees relative to ground-based observations, I compared phenology metrics derived from NPN and PS. The results reveal some general consistency, which suggests that remote sensing data can capture meaningful phenological signals, thereby providing confidence in its use.

However, several important considerations remain when tuning the matching between PS and NPN metrics, particularly due to my limited understanding of the NPN data collection. I would like to consult with domain experts on the following points:

1. **Selection of high-quality NPN data**: To what extent do existing filtering methods enable quality control of NPN data? Is it possible to reliably identify and retain only high-quality observations from individual trees?
2. **Variation in NPN-derived phenometrics**: Does the observed variability in NPN phenometrics primarily reflect real biological and geographical differences, or is it influenced by observation uncertainties for calculating phenological metrics?
3. **Multiple individuals at a single location**: It is common for a single location to have multiple individuals, sometimes even from different species or functional groups. I would like to better understand how those observations from shared locations are generated during NPN data collection.

<!-- # Reference -->

<!-- (1) the timing of spring leaf-out should be no later than 200 in day of year (DOY); (2) the record should have a difference less than 60 days in comparing to VIIRS SOS; and (3) the anomaly of spring leaf-out timing should be less than 30 days within eight years (2013–2020) for an individual plant. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924271622002623) -->

<!-- We used the phenophase “breaking leaf buds” in deciduous vegetation, “increasing leaf size” in evergreen vegetation, and “initial growth (grasses/sedges)” and “increasing leaf size” in stress-deciduous vegetation for evaluating SOS. We used the phenophase “all leaves fallen (deciduous)” in deciduous vegetation and “colored leaves” in stress-deciduous vegetation for evaluating EOS.(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303243420300209) -->

<!-- PhenoCam: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecs2.3912 -->

## Organize data for modeling

```{r}
npn_sos_ps_for_model <- npn_sos |>
  filter(type == "case1") |>
  left_join(
    npn_points,
    by = c("Longitude" = "lon", "Latitude" = "lat")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(city)) |>
  group_by(city, Species) |>
  mutate(
    num_individuals = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(num_individuals >= 30) |>
  select(taxa = Species, site = city, lon = Longitude, lat = Latitude, id = new_id, year, npn_doy) |>
  mutate(direction = "up")

npn_eos_ps_for_model <- npn_eos |>
  filter(type == "case1") |>
  left_join(
    npn_points,
    by = c("Longitude" = "lon", "Latitude" = "lat")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(city)) |>
  group_by(city, Species) |>
  mutate(
    num_individuals = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(num_individuals >= 30) |>
  select(taxa = Species, site = city, lon = Longitude, lat = Latitude, id = new_id, year, npn_doy) |>
  mutate(direction = "down")
  
# Save location into StreetTrees/cleaned_NPN/city.rds
output_dir <- "~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/StreetTrees/cleaned_NPN"
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

npn_sos_ps_for_model |>
  bind_rows(npn_eos_ps_for_model) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  group_split(.keep = TRUE) |>
  walk(function(site_df) {
    site_name <- unique(site_df$site)
    safe_site_name <- site_name |>
      str_replace_all("[^A-Za-z0-9_-]+", "_") |>
      str_remove_all("^_+|_+$")

    write_rds(
      site_df,
      file.path(
        output_dir,
        paste0(safe_site_name, ".rds")
      )
    )
  })
```
